body: The geopolitics of blackboxing: China under the ‘New Cold War’

On November 14, 2022, during the G20 summit, President Biden said to President Xi Jinping there ‘need not be a new Cold War’ between the US and China. The ongoing geopolitics in which we situate our analysis involves the bi-directional US-China geopolitical tensions over ideologies and technology and economic leaderships, fueled by the global COVID-19 epidemiological crisis and surging anti-China sentiments (Sanger, 2021). Under the ‘China Initiative’ (dropped in March 2022 but with lingering repercussions), numerous scholars were arrested on the false charge of ‘IP thefts’ or ‘scientific espionage’ (Subbaraman, 2021). Recently, through the CHIPS Act – which commentators identify as the ‘cold-war era strategy’ – Biden administration tightened restrictions on exchanges and trade of semiconductor technologies, including prohibiting US citizens and residents working for chip plants in China (Mihm, 2022; Herman, 2022). Meanwhile, blaming the US for escalating tensions, China launched ‘Global Security Initiative’ to promote its own vision of global order and partnership (Eguegu, 2022). China’s surveillance industry has been expanding globally at a stunning rate (Huang & Tsai, 2022).

Meanwhile, Chinese tech companies strive to attract transnational venture capitalists by boasting their exceeding wealth of data (e.g., Lee, 2018). Indeed, Chinese data-driven enterprise has benefitted from structural reasons conducive to data accumulation: an enormous population, lax market regulations, the relative absence of public organizing about data privacy, and long-term infrastructural investments from the state (Wu, 2020). This preoccupation with data infrastructures is almost allegorical for us to think about how regulated sanctions and exclusions of datafication are constitutive of knowledge enterprises generically.

Beijing, in particular, has been calling upon Alibaba, Tencent, and Baidu to utilize their existing technological setup and data science experiments to track populations in the name of national security and citizen care (Kim et al., 2021). The persistent weaponization of data infrastructures, which is integral to the ‘tech arms race,’ further focuses societal attention to the pandemic accumulation of digital data.

Meanwhile, COVID-19 has posed severe, but unevenly distributed, material restrictions over China research, scholarly and journalist alike. On top of the increased risks of international border-crossing, China, adhering to a ‘zero-COVID’ policy after reigning in the initial outbreak in a stunning manner, has closed in onto itself with draconian measures. With rare exceptions, obtaining Chinese visas has become a daunting task for non-citizen researchers. Foreign journalists from major press outlets such as New York Times were expelled since the outbreak (Munroe et al., 2020). Those with the access must overcome strenuous and unpredictable testing and quarantine requirements, skyrocketing costs, and extraordinary time commitment to make their way in. These constraints amount to limited physical access to fieldwork, informants, and archives. This level of limitation, some argue, is comparable to what previous generations of Western social scientists experienced prior to China’s reform and ‘opening up’ (Millwood, 2022).

This forms an extraordinary academic ecology when it comes to China, which the broader anglophone discourse projects as an antagonistic and othered state (Siu & Chun, 2020). The conditioning effect is particularly salient in Media and Communication Studies and Information Sciences, which, compared to other social science disciplines, lack the tradition of localized area-specific research (Chakravartty et al., 2018).
